title: Sharing changes with your care team
page_text:
[page 1] Tell the care team about symptoms that are new, keep returning, or are getting worse. A body map can help you name the area: skin, nails, hands, wrists, shoulders, elbows, back, hips, knees, ankles, or feet. Mention fatigue and changes in walking, sleep, work, or self-care. A useful message says where the problem is, when it began, and what has changed. You can say, for example, that new knee pain makes stairs harder.

Before the visit, write your main question and the change that worries you most. Bring your notes so the team can help you decide the next step.

[page 2] A body map cannot tell you how urgent a symptom is. The next lesson explains eye and gut changes to report. Medicine concerns and repeated flares are also reasons to contact the prescribing team. Ask your clinic for its phone number and office hours. Ask about expected response times and how to get help when it is closed. Keep your own care plan available. For urgent symptoms, use urgent medical services rather than waiting for a routine app message.

A sleep record can make the visit more useful. Bring notes on when you sleep, what wakes you, and daytime tiredness. List any recent medicine changes so the team can look for patterns.

title: Eye and gut changes to report
page_text:
[page 1] Eye symptoms can need prompt attention. New eye pain, marked redness, light sensitivity, or blurred sight need urgent assessment. Guidance for possible acute eye inflammation calls for a same-day eye assessment. Seek emergency care for a loss of vision. These symptoms have several possible causes. An examination is needed to find the cause; the app cannot diagnose uveitis from symptoms.

[page 2] Tell the care team about ongoing gut pain, bloating, or changes in bowel habits. Inflammatory bowel disease can occur alongside PsA, but a bowel change does not prove that it is the cause. Describe what changed and when. Your team can decide whether another assessment is needed. If symptoms are severe or you feel acutely unwell, seek urgent medical help. Do not wait for a routine visit to discuss an urgent eye problem.

The reporting guide helps you prepare a clear message. It cannot tell you the cause of a symptom. Use the care guidance above and the instructions from your own team.

title: How doctors assess possible PsA
page_text:
[page 1] There is no single test for PsA. A doctor looks at the whole pattern. This is often a rheumatologist, a doctor for joint and immune system diseases. They ask about your symptoms. They ask if psoriasis or PsA runs in your family. They check your joints, skin, and nails. Swollen or tender joints, psoriasis, and nail changes are important signs.

[page 2] Blood tests help rule out other conditions, such as rheumatoid arthritis. X-rays, ultrasound, or MRI can show changes in joints, the spine, or where tendons attach to bone. See a doctor if joint pain, stiffness, or swelling keeps coming back. Bring a short list of your changes to the visit.

Scene 1: Welcome
- Hi there, and welcome! Today, let’s find out how doctors check for possible psoriatic arthritis, or PsA. [framing]

Scene 2: When to get checked
- See a doctor if you have joint pain, stiffness, and swelling that keeps coming back. [nhs-psa]
- Go even if you do not have psoriasis. These symptoms need to be checked. [nhs-psa]

Scene 3: Meet the rheumatologist
- If your doctor thinks you may have PsA, they will send you to a specialist called a rheumatologist. [nhs-psa]
- A rheumatologist is a doctor who treats joint and immune system diseases. [lesson-text]

Scene 4: No single test
- There is no single test that can prove you have PsA. [niams-care]
- Instead, the doctor puts several clues together: your story, an exam, and some tests. [niams-care]

Scene 5: Your symptoms
- First, the doctor talks with you about your symptoms. [niams-care]
- For example, PsA symptoms can be worse first thing in the morning, and may get better with exercise. [nhs-psa]

Scene 6: Family and skin history
- The doctor will ask if anyone in your family has psoriasis or psoriatic arthritis. [niams-care]
- PsA can sometimes start after a person has had psoriasis for many years. [nhs-psa]

Scene 7: The physical exam
- Next comes a physical exam. [niams-care]
- Swollen or tender joints, psoriasis on the skin, and nail changes are important signs. [niams-care]

Scene 8: Checking the skin
- If you have never been told you have psoriasis, the doctor may check your skin for it. [niams-care]

Scene 9: Where PsA can show up
- PsA can affect the joints, the spine, the skin, and the nails. [src-psa-one-pager-intro]
- It can also affect places where a tendon or ligament attaches to bone, like the back of the heel. [src-psa-one-pager-intro]
- Some people get a whole finger or toe that swells up, like a little sausage. [src-psa-one-pager-intro]

Scene 10: Nail changes
- Nail changes can include tiny dents, called pitting, or a nail that lifts away from the skin underneath. [src-psa-one-pager-intro]

Scene 11: Blood tests
- A blood test helps check for other conditions, such as rheumatoid arthritis. [niams-care]
- Other conditions can also cause joint pain, stiffness, and swelling. Examples are osteoarthritis, rheumatoid arthritis, and gout. [nhs-psa]

Scene 12: Joint fluid test
- Sometimes, a little fluid is taken from a sore joint and tested. [nhs-psa]

Scene 13: Pictures of the inside
- X-rays, ultrasound, or MRI scans can show changes in the joints, the spine, or where tendons attach to bone. [niams-care]

Scene 14: Putting the clues together
- Each test is just one clue. [lesson-text]
- The doctor looks at all the clues together to see the whole pattern. [lesson-text]

Scene 15: Be prepared
- It pays to be prepared. [src-murphys-laws-of-arthritis-preface]
- Problems like a delay in diagnosis can happen, unless we plan ahead. [src-murphys-laws-of-arthritis-preface]
- So bring a short list of your changes, even if they come and go. And note how long stiffness lasts after you wake up. [lesson-text]

Scene 16: Quick review
- Great job! Let’s review. [framing]
- There is no single test for PsA. [key-takeaway]
- Your doctor puts together your story, an exam, and tests. [key-takeaway]
- See a doctor if joint pain, stiffness, or swelling keeps coming back. [key-takeaway]

title: Understanding the CASPAR framework
page_text:
[page 1] CASPAR is a set of rules doctors use to classify PsA. First, there must be inflammation in a joint, the spine, or a tendon attachment. Then other signs are added. Psoriasis you have now counts the most. Psoriasis in the past, or in your family, also counts.

[page 2] Nail changes count. So does a whole finger or toe that is swollen, now or in the past. A negative test for rheumatoid factor (RF) counts. So does new bone next to a joint on an X-ray. A heel spur alone does not count. A score is not a home diagnosis.

- Hi again! Let’s learn about CASPAR. [framing]
- CASPAR stands for Classification criteria for Psoriatic Arthritis. [src-psa-one-pager-intro]
- It comes from a study published in 2006. [src-psa-one-pager-intro]

Scene 2: Sorting the signs
- Doctors use it to sort the signs of PsA into groups. [lesson-text]

Scene 3: Step one is a must
- Step one is a must. [src-mindmap]
- There has to be inflammation in a joint, in the spine, or where a tendon attaches to bone. [src-mindmap]

Scene 4: Step two adds points
- Step two adds points for other signs. [src-mindmap]
- There are five groups of signs. [src-mindmap]

Scene 5: Group 1: Psoriasis
- Group one is psoriasis. [src-psa-one-pager-intro]
- Psoriasis on your skin or scalp right now counts the most. [src-psa-one-pager-intro]
- If you don’t have it now, having had it in the past counts. If you never had it, psoriasis in a close family member counts. [src-psa-one-pager-intro]

Scene 6: Group 2: Nail changes
- Group two is nail changes you have now. [src-psa-one-pager-intro]
- Examples are tiny dents called pitting, a nail lifting off the skin underneath, or thick buildup under the nail. [src-psa-one-pager-intro]

Scene 7: Group 3: The RF blood test
- Group three is a blood test called rheumatoid factor, or RF. [src-psa-one-pager-intro]
- Here, a negative result is the one that counts. [src-psa-one-pager-intro]

Scene 8: Group 4: A swollen finger or toe
- Group four is a whole finger or toe that is swollen, sometimes called a sausage digit. [src-psa-one-pager-intro]
- It counts if it is swollen now, or if a doctor wrote it down in the past. [src-psa-one-pager-intro]

Scene 9: Group 5: New bone on an X-ray
- Group five is new bone forming right next to a joint, seen on an X-ray. [src-mindmap]
- A heel spur alone is not that finding. [lesson-text]

- The reference adds up these points. [lesson-text]
- But a score is not a home diagnosis. [lesson-text]
- A doctor must look at all the findings and check for other causes. [lesson-text]

- Knowing CASPAR can help you follow the conversation with your care team. [lesson-text]

- Nice work! Let’s review. [framing]
- First, there must be inflammation in a joint, the spine, or a tendon attachment. [key-takeaway]
- Psoriasis, nail changes, a negative RF test, a swollen finger or toe, and new bone near a joint can add points. [key-takeaway]
- A score is not a home diagnosis. [key-takeaway]

title: The four pillars of daily care
page_text:
[page 1] Four pillars can help organize daily life with arthritis: Nourishment, Motion, Mastery, and Repose. In plain words, these mean food, movement, coping, and rest. They are a way to plan a discussion about everyday needs. They do not replace medical treatment. This framework is a guide to daily habits. It is not a test of how well your disease is controlled.

The four panels are equal parts of a daily-care plan. Start with the part that matters most to you now.

[page 2] Think about which part of daily life is hardest right now. Food choices, activity, mood, and sleep may each raise different questions. A practical plan can focus on a small change that fits your needs and abilities. The care team can help tailor it. Bring up barriers such as pain, cost, fatigue, or poor sleep. Daily care works best as part of a shared plan, rather than as a test of willpower. Start with one small step you choose with your team. For example, plan a short walk that fits your joints, or set aside time to wind down before bed. Notice how the step fits into your day. You can adjust it as your needs change.

You can plan, choose what matters most, break tasks into smaller parts, and use tools or positions that ease strain. For example, split chores across the week and sit for a task when standing is hard.

title: Movement, coping, and support
page_text:
[page 1] Motion means finding ways to move that fit your joints and current health. Activity plans may include gentle movement, strength, and daily tasks. A physical therapist can help adapt a plan when pain or reduced movement gets in the way. An occupational therapist can suggest ways to protect joints during tasks. Ask your team how to balance activity and rest when symptoms change. Walking, swimming, or cycling may be options. Ask your team which activities fit you before you start. The source also describes strength work and tai chi. You do not need to try every type of exercise.

Try to avoid doing all your chores on a good day and then needing days to recover. Break a large task into short parts, with rest between them. A seated option may help when standing is hard. Ask your therapist to show you a version that fits your joints.

[page 2] Mastery means building ways to cope with the demands of a long-term condition. It does not mean controlling every symptom by thinking differently. Pain, fatigue, and uncertainty can affect mood and confidence. Support from trusted people, a support group, or a trained counselor may help. Tell the care team when worry or low mood affects daily life. Asking for support is part of care, not a sign of failure. A quiet pause or slow breathing may help you make space for stress. These are coping tools. They do not mean that pain is your fault or that you should skip medical care.

Choose a coping step that feels right to you, such as music, writing, or a call to someone you trust. Make a short plan for a hard day while you feel calm. A counselor can also teach skills for coping with pain and worry. Ask for help if low mood affects sleep, work, or taking your medicines.

title: Food, sleep, and recovery
page_text:
[page 1] Nourishment focuses on food and nutrition needs. Food choices need to fit your own health and life. Food does not replace your prescribed PsA care. A dietitian can help with choices that fit your health, budget, and preferences. Ask about supplements or major diet changes before adding them to your care plan. The food chapter discusses vegetables, fruit, and sources of protein. Use these as topics to discuss with your team. It does not mean one food can switch off PsA. The lesson does not ask you to fast or follow a strict diet.

Meals can include a mix of vegetables, fruit, whole grains, and protein foods such as beans, fish, or poultry. The new food tables group meats as Land, Sea, and Sky; poultry and eggs are in Sky. These labels help find foods, not rank them as treatments. Choose foods that fit your needs, allergies, budget, and culture.

[page 2] Repose focuses on rest and sleep. Pain or worry may make sleep harder, and poor sleep can make the next day feel harder to manage. Bring ongoing sleep problems to the care team. Describe whether pain, waking at night, or daytime tiredness is the main concern. Plans for meals, movement, coping, and rest should fit together. The aim is a manageable routine, rather than a strict rule for every day. Try to keep a steady time for bed and waking. A quiet, dark room and a calm wind-down routine may help. Let the team know if pain keeps waking you. Ask for help with sleep rather than changing your medicine on your own.

Keep a short sleep record to share at a visit. Note bedtime, wake time, waking in the night, pain, and how you feel the next day. Tell the team about loud snoring, gasping, or trouble staying awake by day. Good sleep habits may help, but ongoing sleep problems may need more care.

title: What PsA is
page_text:
[page 1] Psoriatic arthritis, or PsA, is a long-term condition linked to inflammation. The immune system becomes overactive. This can cause pain and swelling in joints and where tendons attach to bone. Psoriasis is a related skin condition that can cause scaly patches. Psoriasis and PsA are linked, but they are not the same condition. Many people have skin psoriasis before joint symptoms begin. Some notice joint symptoms first.

A joint is a place where bones meet. Smooth cartilage covers the bone ends. A thin lining makes fluid that helps the joint move. Tendons join muscle to bone. Ligaments join bone to bone. Knowing these parts can help you describe where you hurt.

[page 2] The next lesson groups PsA into six areas, called domains. These are skin, nails, joints away from the spine, the spine, swollen fingers or toes, and tendon attachment sites. You may have changes in some areas and not others. Not everyone has changes in all six areas. Skin and joint changes may follow different patterns. These areas describe the disease. They are not the six topics in this course.

- PsA is a long-term condition that causes inflammation in the joints, and in the places where tendons and ligaments attach to bone. [niams-overview]
- Those attachment places are called entheses. [niams-overview]

Scene 3: An overactive immune system
- In PsA, the immune system becomes overactive, for reasons no one fully understands. [niams-overview]
- This creates inflammation, which leads to pain and swelling. [niams-overview]

- Psoriasis is a related skin condition that can cause scaly patches. [lesson-text]

- On average, PsA starts about 7 to 10 years after skin symptoms begin. [niams-overview]
- But a small group of people notice joint pain before any skin rash. [niams-overview]

Scene 6: Linked, not the same
- So psoriasis and PsA are linked, but they are not the same condition. [lesson-text]

Scene 7: Who gets PsA?
- Anyone can get PsA. It is most common in adults, and it affects men and women equally. [niams-overview]
- Genes play a part. Many people with PsA have family members with the disease. [niams-overview]

- Things like obesity, infection, injury, or stress may help trigger it. [niams-overview]

- Doctors group PsA into six areas, called domains. [src-grappa-domains-in-psa-poster]
- They are skin, nails, joints away from the spine, the spine, swollen fingers or toes, and tendon attachment sites. [lesson-text]

- You may have changes in some areas and not others. Not everyone has all six. [lesson-text]
- Symptoms vary a lot from person to person. [niams-overview]

- There is no cure yet, but treatment can slow the disease, ease pain, and protect your joints. [niams-overview]
- Early treatment is linked to better results, and less damage. [niams-overview]

title: PsA across the body
page_text:
[page 1] The six card labels describe different parts of PsA. Skin psoriasis means scaly skin patches. Nail psoriasis can cause pits or lifting of the nail. Peripheral arthritis affects joints away from the spine, such as those in the hands or knees. Axial disease affects the spine and may involve the joints that join the spine to the pelvis. These are called sacroiliac, or SI, joints.

[page 2] Dactylitis means swelling of a whole finger or toe. Enthesitis means inflammation where a tendon or ligament joins bone. The back or bottom of the heel may be affected. These six domains can help guide treatment discussions. They do not name a drug that is right for you. Eye or bowel inflammation can also occur alongside PsA. These are separate from the six domains. Heart health, blood sugar, weight, and mood can also matter in care. The symptoms topic covers these concerns and changes over time.

The anatomy chart groups the body into nine regions. These are places in the body, not the six PsA domains. For example, the hand has bones, joints, tendons, and nerves. Pain in one area can involve more than one type of tissue.

- Fourth, axial disease. This affects the spine, and may involve the sacroiliac, or SI, joints, where the spine meets the pelvis. [lesson-text]

- Eye inflammation, called uveitis, must be treated quickly to avoid vision loss. [niams-overview]

title: Eyes and symptoms that need prompt care
page_text:
[page 1] The eyes card describes inflammation inside the eye. One name for this is uveitis. It can cause eye pain, redness, blurred sight, or trouble with bright light. These symptoms can have other causes, too. A body map cannot tell which cause is present.

The picture shows the uvea, a layer inside the eye. It includes the iris, the colored part at the front. Uveitis may affect other parts of the eye, too. The picture shows normal parts, so you cannot use it to judge whether an eye is inflamed.

[page 2] New eye pain, marked redness, light sensitivity, or blurred sight need urgent assessment. Possible acute eye inflammation needs a same-day eye assessment. Seek emergency care for a loss of vision. Do not wait for your next routine visit or a reply in the app. An eye exam is needed to find the cause.

title: Related health and changes over time
page_text:
[page 1] The statement above the body map says PsA may lead to lasting damage. Disease activity can rise and fall. A flare is a time when symptoms return or worsen. A flare and lasting joint damage are different. A flare describes activity now; damage refers to changes that may persist. There is no fixed sequence that everyone follows. Treatment aims to control symptoms and limit harm. Tell the team about changes in pain, swelling, fatigue, or daily tasks.

[page 2] A comorbidity means another health condition alongside PsA. This is not the same as joint damage. Your team may discuss heart health, blood pressure, blood sugar, cholesterol, weight, or mood. Some people also have eye or bowel inflammation. Ask which health checks fit your history. A higher risk does not mean you will get another condition. A number on a general poster does not tell you your own risk. Share concerns so the care plan can address your whole health.

The diagram groups health topics you can bring to a visit. It does not rank them or give a personal risk score.

title: Gut and bowel changes
page_text:
[page 1] The gut card describes pain, bloating, and changes in bowel habits. Inflammatory bowel disease, or IBD, can occur alongside PsA. This is a condition that causes inflammation in the gut. A bowel change does not prove that you have IBD or that PsA is the cause.

Use the picture to locate the stomach and the small and large intestine. It shows normal body parts. It cannot show what is causing a change in your bowel habits.

[page 2] Tell your care team about gut symptoms that keep happening. Note what changed, when it started, and how it affects your day. Your team may ask about your medicines and decide whether you need more tests. If symptoms are severe or you feel acutely unwell, seek urgent medical help.

title: Shoulders and reaching
page_text:
[page 1] The shoulders card shows that PsA can affect a shoulder joint and nearby tissues. Pain may make it hard to reach up or put on a shirt. A sore shoulder can have more than one cause. The body map shows a place to discuss, not a diagnosis.

The shoulder is a ball in a shallow socket. A group of muscles and tendons called the rotator cuff helps hold it steady as you lift your arm. Small fluid-filled sacs help tissues glide. The picture shows normal parts, not damage from PsA.

[page 2] Tell your team which shoulder hurts and when the pain began. Describe a task that has become harder, such as reaching a shelf. Mention stiffness, swelling, or a change in how far you can move. Your team can check the joint and the tissues around it.

title: Wrists, hands, fingers, and nails
page_text:
[page 1] This card groups several changes in the hands. A wrist or finger joint may hurt, swell, or feel stiff. Swelling of a whole finger is called dactylitis. It is different from swelling around just one joint. These changes can make tasks such as holding a cup or using buttons harder.

The wrist has small bones between the forearm and hand. Tendons help bend and straighten the fingers. Each finger has a knuckle, middle joint, and end joint. Point to the exact joint or part of the finger that has changed.

[page 2] Nail psoriasis may cause small pits, yellow spots, or a nail lifting from its bed. The photo shows examples of nail changes. Nail changes and joint symptoms do not always happen together. Tell your team whether the change is in a nail, a joint, or the whole finger. Mention any trouble with daily tasks.

title: Feet, heel pain, and tendon attachments
page_text:
[page 1] Enthesitis means inflammation where a tendon or ligament joins bone. The feet card shows this type of change. The Achilles tendon joins the back of the heel. The plantar fascia attaches at the bottom of the heel. These sites can feel sore or tender. The two pictures show the difference in location.

The foot has a heel region, a middle region, and the toes and long bones at the front. A strong band under the foot helps support the arch. Use these landmarks to show whether pain is under the heel, at the back, or near the toes.

[page 2] Tell your team if pain is at the back or bottom of the heel, in a toe, or elsewhere in the foot. Mention whether walking has become harder. Heel pain can have several causes. A symptom picture cannot tell you the cause on its own. Your team can examine the area and decide what to check next.

title: Spine and SI joints
page_text:
[page 1] Axial disease means PsA affects the spine. It may also affect the sacroiliac, or SI, joints. These joints link the lower spine to the pelvis. Inflammation in these areas can cause back pain and stiffness. The spine card shows where these changes may occur.

The spine is a stack of bones called vertebrae. Discs sit between many of them. The sacrum is the bone at the base of the spine. The SI joints link it to the pelvis. The picture shows normal spine regions; it cannot show the cause of your pain.

[page 2] Tell your care team where your back feels sore or stiff. Note when it happens and how it affects sleep or movement. Back pain can have many causes. This map cannot show which cause you have. A clinician uses your story, an exam, and sometimes tests to understand the pattern.

title: Hips and daily movement
page_text:
[page 1] The hips card shows that a hip joint can be affected by PsA. Pain or stiffness may limit movement. You may notice that steps, walking, or getting up from a chair are harder. These examples help you describe a problem; they do not prove that PsA is the cause.

[page 2] Tell your team which side hurts and what has changed. Explain how the pain affects your daily routine. Mention a new limp or trouble doing a task you could do before. The team can check the hip and nearby areas. Do not use the map to decide the cause on your own.

title: Knees, swelling, and stiffness
page_text:
[page 1] The knees card describes swelling, warmth, and stiffness from inflammation. A knee may also hurt. Bending the knee, using stairs, or getting out of a chair may be harder. Knee symptoms can have more than one cause. A picture is only a guide to the area.

The knee joins the thigh bone and shin bone. The kneecap sits at the front. Pads of cartilage help spread the load, while strong bands hold the bones steady. A swollen knee needs an exam; a picture of normal parts cannot show why it is swollen.

[page 2] Tell your care team when the knee problem began and whether one or both knees are affected. Note any swelling and the tasks that have changed. The team may examine how the knee moves and check for other causes. Seek urgent medical help if symptoms are severe or you feel acutely unwell.

title: How treatment goals are chosen
page_text:
[page 1] Treatment discussions start with what is active and what matters to you. The six disease domains help describe this. They include skin, nails, joints away from the spine, the spine, whole-digit swelling, and attachment sites. The care team considers these domains together.

[page 2] Goals may include easing symptoms, protecting joints, and making daily tasks easier. Eye or bowel disease and other health conditions also matter. The team asks what you have tried before. They review your other medicines, side effects, and what matters to you. A treatment plan is chosen for a person, rather than from one symptom alone. A medicine that helps one domain may not cover every concern equally. Ask which parts of your disease the plan addresses and how progress will be checked.

Bring one task you want to do more easily, such as getting dressed or walking to a shop. This gives the team a clear goal to discuss with you.

title: Understanding treatment groups
page_text:
[page 1] Medicines have different jobs. Some help ease pain and swelling. Others aim to control the disease process. These are called DMARDs. Conventional DMARDs act broadly on the immune system. Biologic drugs target selected immune signals. Targeted synthetic drugs act on pathways inside cells. These are names for groups. They do not rank drugs from good to bad. Some drugs are pills. Others are given by a shot or through a vein. How a drug enters the body does not tell you how well it will work for you.

The diagram groups care by its role. The groups can be part of the same plan; they are not steps you move through on your own.

[page 2] A drug is not right for every person or every disease domain. Some plans also include skin care, physical therapy, or help with daily tasks. The benefits, risks, and checks depend on the drug. This lesson does not give doses or tell you to start, stop, or change a medicine. Ask the prescribing team what your drug is for. Ask which checks go with it, too. Make a list of all your drugs and supplements. Ask about blood tests, infection checks, and vaccines that may go with your plan. Keep follow-up visits even when you feel better.

title: Tracking progress and planning for flares
page_text:
[page 1] Follow-up visits look at more than one sign of disease activity. The team may check sore or swollen joints, skin, and tendon sites. They also ask about daily tasks. Your view of pain and health matters, too. Minimal disease activity, or MDA, uses several measures together. It helps track care. It is not a stage of disease. A quiet skin patch alone does not show the whole picture.

[page 2] If symptoms return or worsen, discuss a flare plan with the care team. A short record can note what changed, when it began, and how it affects daily tasks. Ask which changes need a call, which contact route to use, and what to do outside office hours. Repeated flares may mean the plan needs review. Use instructions agreed with your prescribing team for medicine questions. This general lesson does not replace your own flare plan. A useful record can include pain, sleep, energy, mood, and one task that was hard that day. Share patterns at follow-up visits. This can help the team see changes that a single visit may miss.

Use the diagram to plan a short record. You do not need to give yourself a disease score. Ask the team how they want you to share changes.

- Flares are often part of living with psoriatic disease, but they should not happen often when treatment is working. [npf-flares]
- Keeping a record of symptoms and triggers can help you see flares coming. [npf-flares]

Scene 7: A useful record
- A useful record tracks more than pain: also energy, mood, sleep, and how easy daily tasks feel. [src-the-four-pillars-of-arthritis]
- Write down what changed, when it began, and how it affects your day. [lesson-text]

Scene 8: Make a flare plan
- Make a flare plan with your care team. [lesson-text]
- Ask which changes need a call, which contact route to use, and what to do after hours. [lesson-text]

Scene 9: Plan ahead
- It pays to plan ahead for what could go wrong. [src-murphys-laws-of-arthritis-preface]
- Repeated flares may mean the plan needs a review. [lesson-text]

Scene 10: Follow-up visits
- Follow the medicine instructions agreed with your prescribing team. [lesson-text]
- Share patterns at follow-up visits. They can show changes that one visit might miss. [lesson-text]

Scene 11: Quick review
- Great job! Let’s review. [framing]
- Follow-up visits look at more than one sign of disease activity. [key-takeaway]
- If symptoms return or worsen, discuss a flare plan with the care team. [key-takeaway]
